seo.title: Karmic tail 6 5 8 compatibility: love, form and a fair account
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 5 8 compatibility: The Lovers at the entry, The Hierophant in the middle, Justice as the main task — the couple's story told through Beaumarchais.

title: The 6-5-8 karmic tail in compatibility: The Lovers, The Hierophant and Justice
short: In one person's chart, a tail that runs from The Lovers to Justice always has 14, Temperance, in the middle. A couple has 5 there instead — The Hierophant, the card of rites, rules and other people's "that's how it's done". The 6-5-8 karmic tail in compatibility describes the road of two people who chose each other for love: through the form of their union — marriage, families, roles — to the main task, a fair account between the two of them.

paragraphs: Almost everyone knows one of them — The Marriage of Figaro, or Mozart's opera Le nozze di Figaro (1786). But for Beaumarchais it is the middle part of a trilogy about Count Almaviva and his wife Rosine.

The Barber of Seville, or The Useless Precaution (1775): the young Count carries Rosine off from under her guardian's lock and marries her for love. The Mad Day, or The Marriage of Figaro (1784): the marriage is three years old, the Count has cooled towards his wife, and the wedding of his servants Figaro and Suzanne falls apart all day long — right up to a court case. The Guilty Mother, or The Other Tartuffe (1792): twenty years have passed, each of the spouses carries an old fault, and the family has to decide what to do with it.

The actors proposed playing the three pieces on three evenings in a row, as "the whole novel of the Almaviva family", and Beaumarchais approved. In the preface to the third play he explains the plan: on the first day the audience laughed at the Count's "turbulent youth", on the second at "the faults of his manhood", on the third it will see "the picture of his old age". And he adds a sentence worth remembering. Had the drama shown the faults themselves rather than their consequences twenty years on, it would have been called not The Guilty Mother but The Unfaithful Wife, or **The Guilty Spouses**.

The guilty spouses — plural. Love, marriage, a trial — and at the end a guilt that turns out to be shared. That is the 6-5-8 tail, read in order. Matching the trilogy to the cards is our reading; the plot, the court scene and every line quoted below come from Beaumarchais's text (translations from the French are ours).

How far these plays touched the established order we know from a witness. According to the memoirs of Madame Campan, Louis XVI, after hearing The Marriage of Figaro read aloud, said that the Bastille would have to be destroyed before the play could be allowed on stage. It opened all the same, in 1784.

sections.h2: Why the middle is The Hierophant and not Temperance
paragraphs: In a personal matrix the karmic tail follows one formula: the middle equals the entry plus the main task. For 6 and 8 that is 14, Temperance. So nobody has a personal 6-5-8 tail.

In the couple's matrix every point is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The couple's middle is not worked out from the two ends: it is the sum of the two personal middles. Running every date shows that for 6-5-8 couples this sum always goes past 22: in 65% of cases it is 32, in 35% it is 23. Both reduce to 5. Exactly 14 never comes out.

Add up the digits of 14 and you get 5. The couple gets the same Temperance, only spilled over the brim. The Latin temperantia comes from temperare, "to mix in due measure", and in one person the middle of the tail works just like that: he or she blends two sides within. Two people cannot do it that way: between them they need a vessel on the outside — an agreement, a rite, a shared form that both accept. That is The Hierophant. The reading is ours; the arithmetic is the site's engine.

The two ends of the tail, meanwhile, behave as they would in one person. In a personal matrix the entry equals the main task plus the centre. In 98.3% of 6-5-8 couples the centre is The Tower, and 8 + 16 = 24 → 6: the formula holds. Such a couple looks like one person with The Tower in the centre, different only in the middle.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: "to be loved for oneself"
paragraphs: The Barber of Seville opens with the Count hiding under a false name. He calls himself Lindor, a poor bachelor of arts, and stands under Rosine's window because he is tired of conquests "that self-interest, convenience or vanity keep putting in our way". And he says: "How sweet it is to be loved for oneself!"

This is the formula of the entry into the 6-5-8 tail. In Lisovskaya, point M is what the couple strives for, its shared wishes and its "common language". Here the common language is the language of choice: we found each other ourselves, nobody arranged it, we are not like everyone else. You can hear it in how the couple tells the story of how they met, how they guard their private words and rituals, how they defend their right to decide without advisers.

Wen writes of The Lovers that at the start partners have a strong feeling of paradise, but "the feeling of paradise may be evanescent if caution is not observed". Beaumarchais shows how quickly paradise runs into paperwork. At the end of The Barber the notary arrives with two marriage contracts at once: one for the Count and Rosine, the other for her guardian Bartholo and the same Rosine. "The young ladies must be two sisters with the same name," the notary supposes. The contract that gets signed is the one in which Rosine is chosen. Love decides which paper becomes a marriage — but a paper is signed all the same. The entry leads into form.

Point M stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can turn into resistance. In the second play the Count, who once asked to be loved "for himself", explains one night in the garden to his disguised wife (he thinks she is Suzanne) what he looks for elsewhere: "less sameness… now and then a refusal". The wish to choose and be chosen again does not sit easily with what has already been decided. Hence jealousy without love. The Countess throws it at her husband: "Did I unite myself with you to be forever given over to neglect and jealousy — which you alone manage to combine?" Lisovskaya lists among the tasks of the 6 the insecurity from which jealousy and control grow. The Count locks the doors of his wife's rooms and takes the key, while on the same day he arranges a meeting with her maid.

Figaro and Suzanne have the same entry, only a merry one. The play opens with Figaro measuring the floor of their future room with a measuring rod — "nineteen feet by twenty-six" — while Suzanne, at the mirror, pins to her hair the little spray of orange blossom "called the bride's hat". The two are building something of their own. And the first shadow falls at once: the room, the bed and even the dowry are gifts from the Count. The room lies exactly midway between the Count's apartments and the Countess's. Suzanne refuses it and explains to her bridegroom where such generosity comes from: "Did you think, my good boy, that this dowry was for the beaux yeux of your merit?"

sections.h2: Middle of the task: "I am no longer that Rosine"
paragraphs: Three years after the escape from under the lock, the Count says to his disguised wife a sentence that holds the whole move from the 6 to the 5: "I love her very much; but three years of union make marriage so respectable!" Love has become respectable — respected, and far away.

In the second act the Countess answers him herself. In the heat of a quarrel the Count calls her by her name: "Rosine!…" — and hears: "I am no longer that Rosine you pursued so hard! I am the poor Countess Almaviva, the sad, forsaken wife you no longer love." The name under which she was chosen is hidden by a title. This is The Hierophant in the middle of the road: the two begin to live in roles — wife, husband, mistress of the house, head of the family — and the role speaks in place of the person.

Waite sets The Hierophant apart from nature. He belongs to "the world of institution as distinct from that of Nature" and expresses doctrine "when it has passed into the utmost rigidity of expression". In The Marriage of Figaro the institution rules every step. Servants cannot marry without their lord. The old droit du seigneur the Count abolished in public at his own wedding, and now he wants to buy it back from Suzanne in secret. He puts it himself like this: abolishing a shameful right is "only the payment of a debt to decency". Even about love the Count talks in the language of debts, and that is the bridge to the last card.

The other side of The Hierophant is families. Lisovskaya lists among the tasks of the 5 interference from relatives, even in the choice of a partner, and conflict with the partner's family. Beaumarchais takes this to farce. Marceline tries to stop Figaro's wedding through the court — and turns out to be his mother. Wen writes of The Lovers reversed: "meddling from an in-law, relative". Here the meddler is his own mother, who does not yet know it.

Suzanne's uncle, the gardener Antonio, refuses to give his niece "to one who is nobody's child" and lays down the order: in family weddings the parents' wedding goes first. The judge Brid'oison, stammering, answers him with the key line of this card: "Can such a th-thing be, you fool? One is al-always somebody's child." Marceline asks her newly found son: "Did nature never tell you so, a thousand times?" — "Never." Nature is silent; the institution speaks. Figaro sums it up: "All the fools of Andalusia, I do believe, have been let loose against my poor marriage!"

Beaumarchais shows the strength of the 5 as well. In the first act Figaro brings the peasants to thank the Count for abolishing the right and asks him to place on Suzanne, before everyone, the white bridal headdress, "symbol of the purity of your intentions", and to "adopt this ceremony for all marriages". A rite performed before witnesses binds the Count by his own word. "I'm caught," the Count says aside, and postpones the ceremony. This is The Hierophant at its best: a public form holds a promise where feeling alone is not enough.

In the middle of the tail the couple passes exactly here — between the rite that holds the word and the role that takes away the name. This is our reading of point N: Lisovskaya gives it no meaning of its own, it is an "addition" to the main task.

The third act of The Marriage of Figaro is a court hearing, and here the tail reaches its main point. Long ago Figaro borrowed two thousand piastres from Marceline and gave her a written promise. It is read out in court: "…which sum I shall repay her on demand, in this castle, and I shall marry her by way of acknowledgement." Figaro objects: the paper says not "and" but "or". Repay the money — or marry.

The argument is conducted in earnest. Bartholo, counsel for the plaintiff, insists on "the copulative conjunction AND", Figaro on "the alternative conjunction OR". The clerk takes the paper and reads it himself: "AND… OR… AND… OR… The word is so badly written… there's a blot." Then they argue over a comma: "No comma." — "There is one." — "No comma, gentlemen." — "There was one." The fate of a marriage hangs on a conjunction, a blot and a comma.

This is more than a comedy of pettifogging. **"And" or "or" is the central question of Justice for a 6-5-8 couple.** Do love and obligation go together — or does one stand in for the other? Can a debt be paid off with a marriage? Figaro asks whether a man who marries must also pay. "Yes: we marry with separate property," Bartholo replies. "And we with separate persons, since marriage is not a receipt."

The chief task of the 8 in Lisovskaya is to own one's guilt instead of blaming everyone; next to it stand broken promises and debts. Beaumarchais's court shows what happens when this task goes unsolved. The verdict is given by the Count himself: he judges the servant whose bride he wants to take, and rules — pay the two thousand piastres or marry the plaintiff "this very day". "I've won!" Figaro manages to rejoice. "I've lost." And the Count says aside: "At least I am avenged — that's a relief." Among the meanings of Justice reversed Waite names "bias"; the Count shows it in pure form — a judge in his own case.

The voice of the card itself in this scene belongs to Marceline and Figaro. Marceline, reproached all act long for the sins of her youth, tells the judges: "A man who judges us severely here has perhaps ruined a dozen unfortunate girls in his time!" Figaro adds: "The guiltiest are the least generous; that's the rule."

Then comes the moment that makes the act worth reading to the end. Figaro declares that he is a gentleman and cannot marry without the consent of his noble parents, shows a mark on his arm — and Marceline recognises her lost son. Bartholo turns out to be the father. "It's clear: he won't m-marry her," the judge concludes. And Marceline hands Figaro that very paper: "Take back your note — it is yours, it is your dowry."

**The IOU that in the morning could have wrecked the wedding becomes a wedding gift by evening.** The words on the paper are the same. Only one thing has changed: what the people are to each other — parties to a lawsuit, or family. This is what Justice at its best looks like for a 6-5-8 couple: the same account, the same debts and promises, but kept by one's own people, not by opponents.

The fifth act ends with a scene that opera-goers know from two words of Mozart. At night in the garden the Count catches, as he believes, his wife at a rendezvous. He drags the "faithless woman" out before witnesses; one by one everybody kneels and begs for mercy, and the Count answers: "No, no… Not if there were a hundred of you!" Then the real Countess steps out of the other pavilion and kneels too: "At least I shall make up the number."

The Count realises he has spent the whole evening courting his own wife in Suzanne's dress, and pleads: "Only a very generous pardon…" The Countess answers with a line that holds both her character and the whole of the 8: "In my place you would say 'No, no'; and I, for the third time today, grant it without condition." Mozart and da Ponte compress this into "Contessa, perdono" — "Countess, forgive me" — and the reply "Più docile io sono, e dico di sì": "I am gentler, and I say yes."

Back in the second act the Countess had set a condition that is the very measure of Justice: "You ask for yourself a pardon you refuse to others… If ever I agreed to forgive, I would insist that the amnesty be general." One measure for oneself and for the other. The Count lives by a double measure. In the night scene he explains to "Suzanne" that wives must know how to keep their husbands. "So they owe everything?" — "And the man nothing." Among the meanings of Justice reversed Wen names "chauvinism", and here it is in one exchange: an account in which one side owes everything and the other nothing. The gender here is a mark of the eighteenth century, not a rule of the card: in a couple either partner can keep a double measure.

Before the closing songs the Countess hands out the gifts the Count gave the false Suzanne that night in payment for "the right I no longer have": the purse to Figaro, the diamond to Suzanne. "Each shall have what belongs to them." This is almost word for word the ancient definition of justice: to give each their due. And Figaro, who caught the slap meant for the page, grumbles: "That's how the great dispense justice!"

sections.h2: Twenty years later: guilt for two
paragraphs: In The Guilty Mother twenty years have passed. The Countess has a grown son, Léon, and his father is not the Count. The Count has a goddaughter and ward, Florestine, who is in fact his daughter. Each keeps an old fault, and a third person knows both — Bégearss, the friend of the house whom the whole family trusts. In the preface Beaumarchais calls him "the Tartuffe of probity": Molière's Tartuffe dressed up in religion, this one in decency.

Bégearss is a dark Hierophant passing himself off as Justice. A man of "the proper way", through whom the family judges itself, and who profits from the scales never balancing. He frightens the young people into believing they are brother and sister — and very nearly marries Florestine himself.

The resolution is the most exact scene of the 6-5-8 tail in the whole trilogy. When Bégearss is unmasked, the Countess holds out her hand to her husband and asks: "Almaviva! Isn't it true that she is my daughter?" The Count answers: "And he is my son; here are our two children." **Two faults go onto the two pans of the scales at the same moment, and instead of a verdict there is one family.** Justice here is not punishment but balance: nobody weighs the other's fault without setting their own beside it.

In his last long speech the Count says to his wife and children: "There comes an age when decent people forgive each other their wrongs, their old weaknesses… Rosine (it is the name your husband gives back to you), let us go and rest from the labours of the day." The name that the title hid in the second play comes back in the third. The entry — Rosine at the window. The middle — the Countess Almaviva. The main task — Rosine again, but after a fair account.

In the same preface Beaumarchais writes that he composed this drama "with the cool head of a man and the burning heart of a woman". Among the strengths of the 8 in a couple Lisovskaya names "a cool head and a warm heart". The formula is nearly the same, with one difference: in Beaumarchais both halves are held by one person, not shared out between two by role.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: neither partner has Justice
paragraphs: The 6-5-8 tail occurs in about one couple in 47 (2.144%) and ranks 16th of the 97 possible couple's tails. It is built from eight combinations of the partners' personal tails, and running every date turns up three clues in them.

**Neither partner has Justice in their personal tail.** In none of the eight combinations does the 8 stand on any point of a personal tail. The couple's main task is always made of two other cards: 5 + 3 (40% of couples), 5 + 21 = 26 (25%), 4 + 4 (21%), and more rarely 15 + 11, 12 + 14, 16 + 19. Nobody brings Justice in — it appears only as a shared account. Just as in The Guilty Mother, where the scales balance only when both faults are on them.

**The partners carry the other two cards themselves, but not in the tail.** In two couples out of three (65%) one partner has the personal tail 15-20-5, and The Hierophant is their own karmic task. In these couples the other partner has The Lovers in the centre of the personal matrix; across all 6-5-8 couples that is 69%. The layout resembles the trilogy: one has choice and feeling in the centre of the chart, the other has form and rule as a life task. This is not a sharing-out of blame or of roles by gender, but the themes each brings into the union.

**In one couple in five the partners are mirror images.** In 21% of couples both have the same personal tail, 12-16-4, and both have Justice in the centre of the personal matrix. Two Justices in the centres give the couple The Tower (8 + 8 = 16), and the couple's tail is the personal one doubled: 12 + 12 → 6, 16 + 16 → 5, 4 + 4 = 8.
And finally: in a quarter of couples (25.4%) neither partner has a 6, a 5 or an 8 in their personal tail. This tail is not handed to the couple by one of the two — the two make it together.

sections.h2: The Tower in the centre: a mad day
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's matrix is the atmosphere inside the union, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. In 6-5-8 couples it is almost always The Tower (98.3%), occasionally The Chariot (1.7%).

The other title of The Marriage of Figaro is The Mad Day, and it is a good picture of The Tower in the centre. In a single day in the Count's house a dressing-room door is about to be broken in, the page leaps from the bedroom window straight into the flower beds, the gardener demands that the windows "be barred at last", the Countess threatens to retire to the Ursuline convent. By nightfall everything the Count has built on secret rendezvous and convenient verdicts comes down. Waite sees in The Tower not just ruin but "the rending of a House of Doctrine. I understand that the reference is, however, to a House of Falsehood." For a couple with The Hierophant in the middle this is an exact link: the atmosphere of the union tests everything that rests on form without truth.

Lisovskaya sees strength in a couple's Tower too: trials passed together make the union stronger. For the 6-5-8 tail she gives an important detail: such a couple's money rests on strict rules the two have invented together, and that is The Hierophant without anyone else's voice. On the downside she names threats of a break-up used as pressure. The Ursuline convent of the second act is exactly such a threat: spoken to be heard, not in order to leave.
Mozart ended the opera with words that suit this centre: "This day of torment, of caprice and of folly, only love can turn into contentment and joy."

The Chariot in the centre is an atmosphere of movement and victory. Among its reversed meanings Waite lists "Riot, quarrel, dispute, litigation, defeat": even here the tail pulls the couple towards court. Only with The Chariot the formula of the two ends no longer holds: 8 + 7 = 15, not 6.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The World, The Hanged Man, The Empress
paragraphs: The couple's values are the spiritual purpose of the union, the answer to what it exists for. The 6-5-8 tail has three variants, and each answers the tail in its own way. The links below are our reading.

**The World (46.6%).** Waite writes of the garland on The World: according to P. Christian it should be made of roses, "and this is the kind of chain which Éliphas Lévi says is less easily broken than a chain of iron". For a couple that has passed through The Hierophant — through bonds, vows and the "captivity" of his divinatory list — this is the answer: what holds is not the iron of obligation but a chain of roses. The heroine of the trilogy, by the way, has a flower's name.

**The Hanged Man (42.1%).** Wen compares him directly with The Hierophant: The Hierophant is "an orthodox, conventional, institutionalized approach", The Hanged Man is "seeing the same issues as others, but through a different perspective". She also writes that the card has "a component of grace" and that the Seeker must forgive, and, for the reversed card, that "it is not for the Seeker to administer judgment, vengeance, or penance". For a couple with Justice as the main task this is a correction from above: the account is kept honestly, but for the sake of forgiveness, not of a verdict. The Countess who forgives "for the third time today, without condition" lives by exactly this value.

**The Empress (11.3%).** Among the reversed meanings of The Empress Waite lists "the unravelling of involved matters, public rejoicings". That is how every Beaumarchais comedy ends: the knot untied, a wedding, songs. The value here is a fruitful house where tangles are unravelled, not hidden.

sections.h2: Worked example: two people born on the same day
paragraphs: The clearest example is a couple in which both partners were born on 14 April 1975. The site's engine gives this couple the 6-5-8 tail.

Each of them has the same personal matrix: day 14, month 4, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. The karmic task D = 14 + 4 + 22 = 40 → 4. The centre E = 14 + 4 + 22 + 4 = 44 → 8. The entry of the tail M = D + E = 12, the middle N = D + M = 16. The personal tail is 12-16-4, with Justice in the centre.
The couple's matrix adds up the same points of the two personal matrices:
The couple's centre is 8 + 8 = 16, The Tower. The couple's values are 12, The Hanged Man.

In this couple Justice appears three more times: on "What to create together", in "Home and things" and on "Parents together". Lisovskaya advises adding up repeated energies, and four eights give 32 → 5 — the very Hierophant from the middle of the tail. The Tower repeats in "Where it sparks", and The Lovers on "Way into money"; in the relationship sphere the same point M is labelled "Common language".

The doubling shows the mechanics of the tail in pure form. Each of the two, separately, has Justice in the centre of the personal chart. Added to the same date, it moves from the centre to the couple's main task, and The Tower takes its place in the atmosphere of the union.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail
paragraphs: Beaumarchais's trilogy is not a forecast but a picture: a funny first evening, a heavy third and a reconciliation at the end. The 6-5-8 tail does not say what will happen to a couple. It shows the question the two stumble over and what changes the script.
The strong version of this tail is a couple whose form serves love and whose account is kept in the open:

ul: **The name before the role.** The Lovers at the entry are the right to be chosen for oneself. The roles of husband, wife, parents, master of the house are needed, but they do not cancel the person who was chosen. Rosine stays Rosine under a countess's title too.

**A rite to keep one's word, not to hide behind.** The Hierophant is strong when an agreement is spoken aloud and before witnesses, the two alone or with the family, and weak when form covers what goes unsaid. House rules are better invented together than taken ready-made from parents or from "the way people do it".

**"And" or "or" — before signing.** Many quarrels of such a couple are arguments over a conjunction in a sentence both thought they shared. What was promised: both things — or one instead of the other? It is worth settling while there is no blot on the paper.

**Marriage is not a receipt.** Love does not pay off debts, and debts are not collected in love. Money, favours and concessions are more honestly counted separately, so that they do not turn into "look how much I gave you".

**No judging in one's own case.** The Count is ridiculous not because he is jealous but because he judges the servant whose bride he wants to take. In a quarrel between two it helps to check whether one has become the judge in one's own lawsuit.
**One measure for two.** "You ask for yourself a pardon you refuse to others." If forgiving — then with an amnesty for both. If weighing — then putting one's own fault on the scales too.

paragraphs: Beaumarchais gives Suzanne a line as she refuses to argue: "To prove that I am right would be to grant that I could be wrong." Justice begins exactly with that admission. And in Figaro's monologue there is a line the newspaper Le Figaro later took as its motto: "Without the freedom to criticise, there is no flattering praise." For a 6-5-8 couple it is a bridge between the first card and the last. A compliment from The Lovers is worth something only when it sits next to the right to an honest "you're wrong here". And the honest criticism of Justice is borne by those who keep choosing each other.

ul: Beaumarchais: The Barber of Seville, or The Useless Precaution (1775); The Mad Day, or The Marriage of Figaro (1784); The Guilty Mother, or The Other Tartuffe (1792), with its preface "Un mot sur la Mère coupable". Quotations are our translation from the French edition of the Œuvres complètes (Laplace, 1876).
Mozart and Lorenzo da Ponte, Le nozze di Figaro (1786), finale of Act IV.
Madame Campan, Memoirs of the Private Life of Marie Antoinette: Louis XVI's words about the play.
A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1922 reissue): The Lovers, The Hierophant, Justice, The Tower, The Chariot, The World, The Empress.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015): The Lovers, Justice, The Hanged Man.
Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sud'by: sovmestimost' (The Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024): the meaning of the couple's points and of energies 5, 6, 8 and 16.
Calculations and statistics: the site's engine, run over every date of birth.

**M · Entry to the task — 6, The Lovers.** The couple's shared wish is to be chosen for who they are, not for gain, propriety or someone else's will. The two enter the task with this wish, and later the same wish pushes back against any routine.

**N · Middle of the task — 5, The Hierophant.** The road runs through form: ritual, status, families, house rules, the roles of husband and wife. Form keeps a promise — and can hide the person behind it.
**D · Main task — 8, Justice.** To learn to measure oneself and the other by one measure: to own one's share of the blame, to keep promises, not to sit as judge in one's own case.

intro: This road — with a contract, a court case, an ink blot on an IOU and forgiveness at the end — was written down more than two hundred years ago by Beaumarchais. He wrote three plays about one married couple, and they follow the order of these cards.

faq.q: What does the 6-5-8 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's road from love by choice (6, The Lovers, entry to the task), through the form of the union — marriage, families, rules, roles (5, The Hierophant, the middle) — to the main task of a fair account between the two (8, Justice). The couple has to learn to measure themselves and each other by one measure, to keep promises and to own their share of the blame.

faq.q: Why is there no 6-5-8 tail in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the entry plus the main task: 6 + 8 = 14, Temperance. In a couple the middle is the sum of the two personal middles, and for 6-5-8 couples that sum is always above 22 — 23 or 32 — so it reduces to 5.

faq.q: How is the 6-5-8 tail different from the couple's tail 6-14-8?
faq.a: The entry and the main task are the same — The Lovers and Justice. The difference is in the middle: in a 6-14-8 couple the road goes through Temperance, a gradual blending of two characters, and in a 6-5-8 couple through The Hierophant, an outward form: an agreement, a rite, family rules.

No. The first number of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three: every person's personal entry to the tail is a multiple of three, and so is the sum of two such numbers. Running every date shows that only one couple's tail is built from 6, 5 and 8 — 6-5-8.

faq.q: Does the 6-5-8 tail mean a couple needs an official marriage?
faq.a: No. The Hierophant in the middle speaks of form in general: agreements, rites, house rules and relations with families. The tail does not predict events and does not demand a marriage certificate; it shows what the couple passes through on its road and where it has to learn a fair account.

report: It took Beaumarchais three plays and twenty years of stage time to give his heroine back her name. In The Barber of Seville Count Almaviva falls in love with Rosine and carries her off from under her guardian's lock. In The Marriage of Figaro, in the third year of their marriage, she tells him in the middle of a quarrel: "I am no longer that Rosine… I am the poor Countess Almaviva, the sad, forsaken wife." In The Guilty Mother the Count at last says: "Rosine (it is the name your husband gives back to you)." Between these lines lies the 6-5-8 tail: The Lovers at the entry, The Hierophant in the middle, Justice as the main task.

report.h3: First, to be chosen for oneself

report: The Count began in disguise. He called himself Lindor, a poor bachelor of arts, because he was tired of conquests "that self-interest, convenience or vanity keep putting in our way". And he said: "How sweet it is to be loved for oneself!" This is the entry of a couple with this tail — a shared wish to be chosen as a person, not for a title, for gain or as a convenient option. Hence the couple's common language: we found each other ourselves, we are not like everyone else.

But at the end of the same play the notary arrives with two marriage contracts for one Rosine — one for the Count, the other for the guardian. Love decides which of them gets signed, yet what is signed is still a paper. The entry leads into form. And the same wish to be chosen later pushes back against what has been settled: three years on, the Count looks elsewhere for "less sameness… now and then a refusal".

report.h3: When the role speaks for the person

report: "I love her very much; but three years of union make marriage so respectable!" the Count admits. Love has become respectable — respected, and far away. This is The Hierophant in the middle of the road: the two begin to live in the roles of wife, husband, master of the house, and the role speaks in place of the person. Waite places this card in "the world of institution as distinct from that of Nature". In The Marriage of Figaro the institution rules every step: servants cannot marry without their lord, the bride's uncle will not give her "to one who is nobody's child", and the wedding is nearly stopped in court by a woman who turns out to be the bridegroom's mother.

In one person the middle of such a tail would hold Temperance — the ability to blend two sides within oneself. Two people need a vessel on the outside: an agreement, a rite, a rule that both accept. The Hierophant has a strong side too. Figaro asks the Count to place the bridal headdress on Suzanne before everyone and to "adopt this ceremony for all marriages", and the public form binds the Count by his own word. **Form either keeps the word or takes away the name**, and the middle of the tail runs exactly between the two.

The central scene is the trial in the third act. Long ago Figaro borrowed money from Marceline and wrote that he would repay the sum "and marry her". He claims the paper says "or". The clerk reads it aloud: "AND… OR… AND… OR… The word is so badly written… there's a blot." Then they argue over a comma. **The fate of a marriage hangs on a conjunction, a blot and a comma** — and this is the central question of Justice for a couple with this tail: do love and obligation go together, or does one stand in for the other? Figaro answers with a formula: marriage "is not a receipt".

The verdict is given by the Count, a judge in his own case: he judges the servant whose bride he wants to take, and lets drop aside: "At least I am avenged — that's a relief." Among the meanings of Justice reversed Waite names "bias". Then Marceline recognises Figaro as her lost son and hands him that very paper: "Take back your note — it is yours, it is your dowry." **The IOU that in the morning could have wrecked the wedding becomes a wedding gift by evening.** The words are the same. Only one thing has changed: what the people are to each other — parties to a lawsuit, or family.

report.h3: Two faults on one pair of scales

report: All through the mad day the Count lives by a double measure: wives, he says, must know how to keep their husbands. "So they owe everything?" — "And the man nothing." The Countess sets a different condition: "You ask for yourself a pardon you refuse to others… If ever I agreed to forgive, I would insist that the amnesty be general." At the end, realising he has spent the whole evening courting his own wife in another woman's dress, the Count begs for mercy. She answers that "for the third time today" she grants it "without condition". And as she hands out his night-time gifts, she speaks the ancient formula of justice: "Each shall have what belongs to them."

Twenty years later each of the spouses carries an old fault: the Countess has a son who is not her husband's, the Count a ward who is in fact his daughter. The resolution is the most exact scene of this tail. The Countess asks: "Almaviva! Isn't it true that she is my daughter?" The Count answers: "And he is my son; here are our two children." **Two faults go onto the two pans at the same moment, and instead of a verdict there is one family.** Only after that does Rosine become Rosine again.

The strong version of the tail rests on a few simple things: the name before the role; a rite to keep one's word, not to hide behind; "and" or "or" settled before signing, not after the blot; one measure for two — owning one's share of the blame before weighing the other's. Beaumarchais wrote a line that the newspaper Le Figaro later took as its motto: "Without the freedom to criticise, there is no flattering praise." A compliment from The Lovers is worth something only next to the right to an honest "wrong here". And a fair account is borne by those who keep choosing each other.

unit.title: Marriage is not a receipt

captions.M: To want to be chosen for who you are
captions.N: To pass through roles and rites without losing your names
captions.D: To measure yourselves and each other by one measure

unit.meaning: Your task is a fair account with no double measure: keep your word, own your share of the blame, never judge your own case.
